statement: An online/offline indicator shows, for each user in a list, a dot that is green when the user is online and grey when offline.

speaker: teacher
verbatim: Online Offline Indicator user 1 user 4 user 5 user 3

statement: Since it is day 1, the design is kept simple and does not focus much on scaling; scaling is covered later in the course.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Note: Since it is day 1, we keep thing simple and do not put a lot of focus on Scaling

statement: To approach system design, decide the core of the system and build the system around it (spiral).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Approaching System Design: Decide the core & build your system around it

statement: The core is use-case specific, e.g. the database or communication.
detail: Right-hand text cut off at the page edge after 'Database, communicatio'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Core is use-case specific Database, communicatio

statement: Incremental building: 1) start with a day-zero architecture, 2) see how each component behaves under load and at scale, 3) identify the bottleneck, 4) re-architect, 5) repeat (loop back to step 2).
detail: Board writes 'architechure' [sic].
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Incremental building 1. start with a Day Zero architechure 2. See how each component would behave ... 3. identify the bottleneck 4. re-architect 5. repeat

statement: First storage model: map each user (int) to online/offline (bool); which database to use is not yet decided.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Storage: user -> online/ offline int bool [not yet decided] We still have not picked which DB to use

statement: The access pattern of the online/offline indicator is key-value.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Access : Key Value

statement: The get-status API takes a batch of user ids in one request: GET /status/users?ids=u1,u2,u3,u4 (user -> API server -> database).
detail: The brace label reads 'user ids for whom status need to be fixed' (probably meant 'fetched').
speaker: teacher
verbatim: GET /status/users ? ids = u1 , u2 , u3 , u4 user ids for whom status need to be fixed

statement: Status is updated with a push-based model: users push their status periodically.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Push based model : Users push their status periodically

statement: API servers cannot pull status from clients because the server cannot proactively talk to a client, unless there is a persistent connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Our API servers cannot "pull" from client because we cannot proactively talk to client * unless there is a persistent connection

statement: Every user periodically sends a heartbeat to the service: POST /heartbeat marks the authenticated user as alive.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every user periodically sends "heartbeat" to the service POST /heartbeat -> the authenticated user will be marked as "alive"

statement: A user is offline when no heartbeat has been received for long enough; how long is 'long enough' is subjective.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So, when is a user offline ? When we did not receive "heartbeat" for long enough Subjective!

statement: The offline threshold is handled through business logic, e.g. 30 seconds without a heartbeat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Offline : When we do not recieve heartbeat long enough Handling through business logic say 30 seconds

statement: In the database, store the time the last heartbeat was received: table pulse(user_id, last_hb).
detail: Example rows u1 1000, u2 1050, u3 1060.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: In database store "time you received the last heartbeat" pulse user_id last_hb

statement: On each heartbeat: UPDATE pulse SET last_hb = NOW() WHERE user_id = u1, with NOW() in epoch seconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: UPDATE pulse SET last_hb = NOW() WHERE user_id = u1 epoch seconds

statement: The user sends a heartbeat every 10 seconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: * User sends heartbeat every 10 seconds

statement: GET /status/<user_id>: if there is no entry for the user, return offline; if the entry's last_hb is older than NOW() - 30 sec, return offline; otherwise online.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if no entry in the database for user -> offline if entry and entry.last_hb < Now() - 30sec -> offline Online

statement: Each pulse entry has two int columns (user_id, last_hb) of 4 bytes each, so 8 bytes per entry; entries grow one per user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Each entry has 2 colum user_id , last_hb int (4B) int (4B) Size of each entry = 8B

statement: For 1 billion users (1B entries) total storage is 8 GB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Total storage required for 1B entries = 8 GB

statement: Requirement check for storage optimisation: all the product cares about is online or offline per user.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Can we do better on storage ? Requirement : ... all we care is online/ offline

statement: Treat absence as offline: if the user is not present in the DB, return offline, and expire (delete) entries after 30 seconds.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what if absence == offline ? Idea: if user not present in the DB, we return offline. So, let's expire the entries after 30 seconds

statement: Deleting entries saves space by not storing data of inactive users, so total entries equal active users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if we delete entries -> we save a bunch of space by not storing data of inactive users Total entries = Active users

statement: With 1B total users and 100k active, total entries are 100k and total size is 800 KB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if 1B total users and 100k active then total entries = 100k total size = 800KB

statement: Approach 1 for auto-delete, a CRON job that deletes expired entries, is not a robust solution and needs edge cases handled in business logic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Approach 1: Write a CRON job that deletes expired entries - Not a robust solution - we need to handle edge case ...

statement: Approach 2 for auto-delete: offload expiry to the datastore.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Approach 2: Can we not offload this to our datastore ?

statement: Never re-invent the wheel.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Never re-invent the wheel !

statement: Databases with key-value plus expiration, such as Redis and DynamoDB, fit this use case.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: DB with KV + expiration -> Redis -> DynamoDB

statement: On receiving a heartbeat, update the entry in Redis/DynamoDB with ttl = 30 sec; every heartbeat moves the expiration time forward.
detail: At 00:44:30 the board reads 'heartbead' [sic], fixed to 'heartbeat' by 00:44:45.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Upon receiving an heartbeat - update entry in Redis/ DynamoDB with ttl = 30 sec Every heartbeat move the expiration time forward !

statement: Redis vs DynamoDB for the indicator: persistence is a point for DynamoDB.
detail: Board writes 'persistnce' [sic]; tick in the DynamoDB column.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis DynamoDB ✓ —— persistnce

statement: Redis vs DynamoDB: DynamoDB is managed, which matters depending on team size and expertise.
detail: Board: 'managed (* team size)' with '& experte' (cramped, reads as 'expertise') below it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ✓ —— managed (* team size) & experte

statement: Redis vs DynamoDB: vendor lock-in (cost, issues) is a point for Redis.
detail: Board: 'vender lockin (cost/ issue/' [sic], parenthesis left open.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ✓ —— vender lockin (cost/ issue/

statement: Redis vs DynamoDB: future extensibility is a point for Redis.
detail: Written in a scrawl; audio at 00:57:39 says 'future extensibility'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ✓ —— future extensibility

statement: Redis vs DynamoDB: time sensitivity is a point for Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: ✓ —— time sensitivity

statement: When choosing between the two datastores, also do a cost estimation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Which one would you pick & why ? * Cost Estimation

statement: In the real world WebSockets are used in such systems; this design uses HTTP heartbeats because it is day 1.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Note: In real world, WebSockets are used in such systems, but this is Day 1, hence we keep things simple.

statement: With a heartbeat every 10 seconds, one user sends 6 heartbeats per minute; 1m active users give 6m requests per minute, each causing one DB call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Heartbeat is sent every 10 seconds So, one user in 1 minute sends 6 heartbeats ... 6m req/min

statement: The DB therefore needs to handle 6m updates per minute.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Our DB needs to handle 6m updates per minute !!

statement: These are micro reads/updates, hence the network becomes the bottleneck.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: micro reads/ updates Hence n/w bottleneck

statement: Creating a new DB connection every time is the costly part; a connection pool keeps pre-established connections between the server and the DB.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What's hectic ? creating a new connection everytime Connection Pool pre-established connections

statement: A similar system to the online/offline indicator: failure detection in a distributed system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Similar Systems : - Failure detection in a distributed system

statement: Soft delete: when a user deletes a blog, instead of a DELETE the system does an UPDATE that sets is_deleted.

case_study: Multi-user blogging platform (Medium.com) designed in the second half.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Key reasons: Recoverability, Archival, Audit

statement: Soft delete is also easier on the database engine because there is no tree re-balancing.
